sittings.bodyEn: Call the idea validated when three separate people have paid you inside two days. It protects your time and cash, proves you can find buyers, puts money in first, and forces you to move. Describe the offer, ask which version they want, and request payment now, with delivery named for later. A short note can show the price per day, sell a block of several months, cap the batch, and ask who else buys snacks for an office. After the money arrives, find people who already make the product and buy from them at the prices in your model. The dangerous order is a stocked product that nobody has paid for. Expect a few weekends of repeats, so one miss can send you into the next test without a year of theory.

terms.hook: Three people pay you within forty-eight hours for an idea.

sittings.bodyEn: Success in this window means moving fast and spending as close to nothing as you can. Forty-eight hours pushes you to invent and quiets the voice that wants another week of doubt. The first customer is often a friend, the second is often family, and the third is the hard one. You are validating an idea, and if three payments are difficult now they will be more difficult later. A promise to pay later is a soft refusal, so collect real money from a real person. A pay app or cash is enough to make the yes official. You are measuring excitement about the help you offered, and a yes you had to invent is a weak signal.

terms.hook: Three paying customers, forty-eight hours, and money collected up front.

sittings.bodyEn: The first method is direct preselling: meet a real person, say what you are offering, ask for money, and watch what they do. A two-sentence door offer can name a problem you can see and offer a free estimate, and that shape has started real service businesses. Message people who already live with the problem, including a group you belong to, and ask them to pay for the help. The first payments can arrive before a website, a prototype, a company bank account, or a legal filing exists. State the problem in one plain line so the talk stays on their pain. Ask what they do today and what is wrong with that current fix. Then decide how you will prove they will pay, and go collect that proof inside the week.

List ten ideal people to presell, chosen because they are the easiest likely buyers and the fastest path to a first dollar. Use columns for name, company, phone, email, when you contacted them, when you will follow up, and notes. Start with close friends who might care, inside the circle you already have, because reaching past them is often a way to dodge a no. Pull names from friend lists, groups, favorite contacts, old coworkers, past clients, text threads, a faith community, and followers who fit. For an office snack, that list might be health-conscious friends, people who work in offices, and service providers you already pay. Ten lines is the minimum before you start the asks. If you cannot name ten people who could buy, choose another idea you can actually reach.

terms.hook: Ten named people you can contact now who fit the offer.

sittings.bodyEn: Treat validation as a conversation for learning whether you can help and whether they will pay. With people who know you, keep the talk exploratory so you can hear what excites them and adjust the offer. Listen first and get them talking about the problem. Ask what is most frustrating about the current situation, how a fix would make life better, and what they think the fix should cost. Repeat their problem back in one sentence so they can hear that you understood. Prefer questions that start with what or how, because a why or a yes-or-no question closes the learning. Write the pain down, because a larger pain is a larger chance they will pay.

terms.hook: Ask about the frustration, the improvement, and the price, then repeat what you heard.

sittings.bodyEn: Once the pain is clear, offer a few ways you could solve it and watch which one they would pay for. Two or three concrete shapes are enough, such as a lesson they do alone or a visit where you do the work. Energy and a willingness to pay are the signals you want, and a flat face means low interest. Move to the sale when you know which option lit them up. Put the price, the result, and the timing in one line, and ask if you can do it today. A comparison helps them decide: you are like the familiar option, with one difference they care about. Payment means the idea passed, and a refusal still gives you a chance to learn from the no.

terms.hook: A few ways you could solve the pain, offered so you can see which one they want.
The moment a warm option becomes a price they can pay today.
Price, result, and timing spoken together in one sentence.

sittings.bodyEn: People stay interested until money is due, so skip the question that only asks whether they are interested. Ask them to pay immediately. You can sell before the thing is fully made if you say clearly when it will arrive. Advance payment is reasonable once that delivery expectation is plain. One sturdy version is a today-only price they keep if they join now. After the first buyers pay, write them for feedback you can use to improve the offer. Money in hand is the yes this challenge counts.

Preselling produces plenty of noes, and each no is a chance to learn the problem more deeply. Ask why they refused, because the criticism you fear is the information you came for. Ask for one specific person they know who would really want this, and use a number so the referral stays concrete. Ask what would make the offer an easy yes, in case a neighboring product is the real demand. Ask what they would pay for that neighboring thing, because an early price is hard to set and their number helps. One poster nobody wanted turned into a shirt people already reacted to, and a photo plus a price collected orders before a maker was hired. Use a call, a text, or a direct message, because a public post you hope someone notices is the slower route.

terms.hook: Why they refused, who else would want it, what would make it easy, and what they would pay.

sittings.bodyEn: The second method puts the offer where people are already trying to spend, such as classifieds, a community marketplace, or a forum. Post a similar item, or a rough picture of an item that does not exist yet, and attach a price. A camera listed for rent can collect a fee within hours, at the cost of the post alone. A photo of a close version, a line about a small batch, and a pay link can sell custom goods before you hire anyone to make them. After the orders exist, find a maker and ship what people already bought. A plain social note can do the same for a skill: say what you already do well, invite a few people to reply, and charge for a session such as shadowing you at work. That sequence beats a logo, a domain, and a search for customers who were never looking.

A landing page plus ads is the third method, and it comes last because the setup and the ad work are slow and costly. If you use it, stop the work at forty-eight hours so the ads cannot eat the weekend. A cheap domain, a plain page, a simple mark, and a price that still leaves profit are enough. Send the order button to a checkout that pays you directly, and describe the product in ordinary words. A small ad test can bring real payments even when designers would dislike the page. Judge the test by the payments. The name, the layout, and the polished sentences can wait, because a purchase is the signal that the offer is real.

Reach those ten people in whatever channel answers fastest: a call, a text, an email, or a private message. Open by recalling something they already like, name the offer, and ask them to be a first customer at a clear price. Answer what the product is, offer a refund if they dislike it, and decline a vague promise to pay later. Cap the first batch so you can place one real supply order, and ask them to send money now to hold the spot. If nobody pays, choose another idea and return to finding problems. If at least three people pay, you have a business and the next conversation is how it grows. Finish inside forty-eight hours so the limit stays the thing that makes you inventive.

A validated idea is three real payments, collected during a two-day window, before you build. Start with ten named prospects and a talk that listens, offers choices, and then states price, result, and timing. Ask for money today, including before the product is finished, and say when it will arrive. On a no, ask why, who else, what would make it easy, and what they would pay. You can also post a priced offer where buyers already browse, or run a plain page for no longer than two days. Suppliers and stock come after the money. Zero payments sends you back to a new idea, and three payments means the weekend produced a business.
